text: {"headline":"Provider 1000000213 bills 99215 well above risk-adjusted expectation in every complexity tier, but only two 99215 claims have records, so documentation is too thin to separate upcoding from a sicker panel.","leaning":"inconclusive","interpretation":"The 99215 excess is not confined to simple patients. The provider's 99215 share runs above the all-provider share in every condition tier, with the largest gap among patients with 5+ conditions, which partly fits a complex panel. But the elevated shares at 1–2 conditions, and sampled 99215s on patients with no chronic conditions billed for follow-up or minor complaints (e.g., C0104898 with Z09, C0105648, C0106831), are the part that needs explaining. The same patient, M0044589, appears with both a 99215 (C0106831) and a 99213 (C0105630) for similar complaints. Documentation does not settle it. The two documented 99215s (C0104723, C0107148) both support high MDM, and only 1 of 22 moderate-or-higher data-reviewed notes lacked a lab or test line, which is a weak signal at most. The below-billed rates on documented 99213 and 99214 claims sit above peer rates, but those counts are small and noisy. A reviewer should first request charts targeted at the low-complexity 99215 claims listed in the packet, to see whether high MDM or qualifying time is actually documented, and should compare those against the provider's 99213 and 99214 notes for the same patients."}
